fields.meta_title: Gmail Automation for Invoices, Leads, and Support | Emergent
fields.meta_description: Build Gmail automation that reads invoice emails into records, routes leads, follows up on quotes, and escalates unanswered support email.
fields.h1: Build Gmail Automation That Goes Past Filters
fields.hero_description: Build Gmail automation that turns each incoming email into a record with an owner and a deadline, in a database you own.
fields.features_heading: What the App Does With Each Email
fields.features_subheading: Emergent builds the whole Gmail workflow from one prompt, with the records it writes and the screen your team works from.
fields.feature_1:
Starts the moment an email lands

Connects to your Gmail account through its API. Each new message starts a run, and the app sorts it by who sent it and what the subject line says before any rule acts on it.
fields.feature_2:
Reads attachments into fields

An AI step turns an attached invoice or receipt into fields such as vendor, amount, and due date. Any value the AI is unsure of goes to a teammate to confirm before the record saves.
fields.feature_3:
Gives every email an owner

You write the routing rules, such as the team size in an inquiry or the sender's domain. The app sends each email to the right person by Slack or email alert and records who has it.
fields.feature_4:
Chases the replies that never came

Set how many days a sent quote or request can sit without an answer. The app sends a follow-up from your own address in the same thread, then alerts you if that goes quiet too.
fields.feature_5:
Keeps every thread in your database

Each email the app handles becomes a row with its status and the person who owns it right now. The data sits in a database you own, and there is no cap on the tasks it runs.
fields.feature_6:
Your Gmail app's code, in GitHub

Export the full code to your GitHub repository on paid plans. A developer can read every routing rule and API call, and change how the app treats a sender without starting over.

fields.tab_content_1:
Dagny signs off on any field under 90%

Invoices reach Hollinshead Joinery's accounts inbox as attachments. The app reads INV-4471 from Ferrovale Timber into vendor, invoice number, total, and due date. Any field read under 90% confidence waits for bookkeeper Dagny Lowenfeld, and the due date is one. Once she confirms, the $2,840.00 bill is saved.
fields.tab_content_2:
Teams of 10 or more reach sales the same hour

Saoirse Valdane emails Marlowgate Coworking's sales inbox about desks for her team of 14. The app saves her company, team size, and start month to a new lead. Any inquiry for 10 or more people goes to sales lead Tobiah Renquist by Slack direct message. Smaller teams stay in the sales inbox.
fields.tab_content_3:
Unanswered after 3 days means a second email

Yusra Pembleton sends quote Q-2318 for $6,450 to Pennacrest Dental from her Gmail account, and the app logs it against the thread. With no reply after 3 days, the app sends a short follow-up from her account in the same thread. If 7 days pass with nothing back, the quote is marked cold and Yusra gets an alert.
fields.tab_content_4:
After 4 quiet hours, Ruairi gets the ticket

Each email to Cobblefield Bike Hire's support address gets an automatic reply with a ticket number. Ticket #5126, about a bike lock that will not open, has had no answer for 4 hours. Any ticket quiet that long goes to support lead Ruairi Delacroix by Slack direct message, with the customer's email attached.

fields.howto_description: Seven steps to set up Gmail automation for one inbox, test it on real mail, and then move on to the next inbox.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Pick the inbox that eats the most time
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Note what happens to each email
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Connect Gmail and your other tools
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Set the numbers each rule uses
fields.howto_step_1_des: List the shared addresses and personal inboxes your team reads each day, such as accounts or support. Count a normal week of mail in each. Start with the inbox where someone retypes email into another system, because that is where errors and delays pile up.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Take ten recent emails from that inbox and note what someone did with each one: where the details went and who got told. Those notes become the rules. An email nobody acted on belongs in a filter, not an app.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Give the app access to the Gmail account through its API, along with the tools the email ends up in: your accounting system or CRM. Use a shared address for team inboxes. Then the workflow never depends on one person's login.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Every rule needs a number someone agreed to. Think of the confidence below which a person checks an extracted field, the team size that counts as a large lead, the days before a follow-up, the hours before an escalation. Write them down before you build.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Describe the workflow in a prompt
fields.howto_step_5_des: Tell Emergent which inbox to watch, what to pull from each email, where to save it, and who hears about the exceptions. Emergent builds the workflow and the database behind it. You change any rule later by prompting, without starting over.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Write five emails from a second account that match the cases in your notes, including one that should reach a teammate. Check that each one lands on the right record, that the reply reads well, and that the alert reaches the person you named.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Review the hand-offs for two weeks
fields.howto_step_7_des: Read every email the app passed to your team and every one it handled alone. Where it handed off something your records could answer, add that rule by prompting. When the hand-offs settle, move to the next inbox on your list.

faq_plan.a: Gmail automation is software that acts on email in a Gmail account without a person doing each step. It can pull details out of a message or alert the right teammate. Filters inside Gmail cover the sorting. An app linked to the account through the Gmail API can also carry each email into your books or your CRM.

faq_plan.q: How do I set up Gmail automation?
faq_plan.a: Start with one inbox and write down what a person does with each email in it today. Then describe the trigger, the details to save, and who handles the exceptions to Emergent's AI automation builder. Emergent builds the workflow and its database, linked to the Gmail account you choose. Try it with a few emails from a spare address before you switch it on.

faq_plan.q: Can Gmail automation send an automatic reply to every new email?
faq_plan.a: Yes, though the vacation responder is the wrong tool for it. In most cases, Gmail's vacation responder sends its reply only the first time a person messages you. For a reply to every message, such as a ticket number on each support request, the app sends its own reply to each new email and logs it on the ticket.

faq_plan.q: Can Gmail automation alert my team when an important email arrives?
faq_plan.a: Yes. You decide what makes an email important: a sender's domain, a word in the subject line, or an order value in the body. The app then alerts the person who owns that kind of email by Slack, email, or in-app message. Add a reminder for anything still unanswered after a set number of hours, and an escalation to a manager after that.

faq_plan.q: Can Gmail automation read invoice attachments?
faq_plan.a: Yes. An AI step reads the invoice or receipt attached to an email into structured fields, such as the vendor and the total. Set a confidence bar per field, and anything below it waits for a person to confirm. Emergent can build the app so each invoice and the email it came in sit together in a database you own.

faq_plan.q: How does Gmail automation know a new email has arrived?
faq_plan.a: Through push notifications. The Gmail API uses the Cloud Pub/Sub API to deliver push notifications when the mailbox changes, and the app then reads the new message. The app also has to renew its watch on the mailbox. Google's guide says to call the watch method at least once every 7 days, or the updates stop.

faq_plan.q: Where do filters fall short in Gmail automation?
faq_plan.a: Filters act on the message and nothing else. They can send email to a label, or archive, delete, star, or automatically forward your mail. Work that happens outside the inbox needs an app, such as saving an invoice to your books or chasing a quote nobody answered. Emergent builds that app from a plain-English prompt, and you change its rules the same way.

faq_plan.q: Can Gmail automation follow up when a client does not reply?
faq_plan.a: Yes. The app logs each sent quote or request with its thread. If no reply arrives within the number of days you set, it sends a follow-up from the sender's own account in that same thread. Stop at one or two follow-ups. After that, mark the item cold and tell the sender.

faq_plan.q: Can Gmail automation search old emails the way the search box does?
faq_plan.a: Yes. The message list in the Gmail API supports the same query format as the Gmail search box. A search your team already runs in Gmail works for the app too. Use it once at the start to pull last quarter's invoices or open inquiries into the new records, and the workflow takes over from there.

faq_plan.q: Does Gmail automation keep a record of every email it handles?
faq_plan.a: It should, and the app Emergent builds keeps one. Every handled message gets a row with its sender, what the app did, and who owns it now. That record lives in a database you own. A question about a missed reply months later still has an answer. Pull up the rows whenever your auditor or a new teammate asks for the history.
